CHAPTER LXXXI

THE HEARTH

“Eli,” said Catherine, “answer me one question like a man, and I'll ask
no more to-day. What is wormwood?”

Eli looked a little helpless at this sudden demand upon his faculties;
but soon recovered enough to say it was something that tasted main
bitter.

“That is a fair answer, my man, but not the one I look for.”

“Then answer it yourself.”

“And shall. Wormwood is--to have two in the house a-doing nought, but
waiting for thy shoes and mine,” Eli groaned. The shaft struck home.

“Methinks waiting for their best friend's coffin, that and nothing to
do, are enow to make them worse than Nature meant. Why not set them up
somewhere, to give 'em a chance?”

Eli said he was willing, but afraid they would drink and gamble their
very shelves away.

“Nay,” said Catherine, “Dost take me for a simpleton? Of course I mean
to watch them at starting, and drive them wi' a loose rein, as the
saying is.”

“Where did you think of? Not here; to divide our own custom.”

“Not likely. I say Rotterdam against the world. Then I could start
them.”

Oh, self-deception! The true motive of all this was to get near little
Gerard.

After many discussions and eager promises of amendment on these terms
from Cornelis and Sybrandt, Catherine went to Rotterdam shop-hunting,
and took Kate with her; for a change, They soon found one, and in a good
street; but it was sadly out of order. However, they got it cheaper for
that, and instantly set about brushing it up, fitting proper shelves for
the business, and making the dwelling-house habitable.


Luke Peterson was always asking Margaret what he could do for her. The
answer used to be in a sad tone, “Nothing, Luke, nothing.”

“What, you that are so clever, can you think of nothing for me to do for
you?”

“Nothing, Luke, nothing.”

But at last she varied the reply thus: “If you could make something to
help my sweet sister Kate about.”

The slave of love consented joyfully, and soon made Kate a little cart,
and cushioned it, and yoked himself into it, and at eventide drew her
out of the town, and along the pleasant boulevard, with Margaret and
Catherine walking beside. It looked a happier party than it was.

Kate, for one, enjoyed it keenly, for little Gerard was put in her
lap, and she doted on him; and it was like a cherub carried by a little
angel, or a rosebud lying in the cup of a lily.

So the vulgar jeered; and asked Luke how a thistle tasted, and if his
mistress could not afford one with four legs, etc.

Luke did not mind these jeers; but Kate minded them for him.

“Thou hast made the cart for me, good Luke,” said she, “'Twas much. I
did ill to let thee draw me too; we can afford to pay some poor soul for
that. I love my rides, and to carry little Gerard; but I'd liever ride
no more than thou be mocked fort.”

“Much I care for their tongues,” said Luke; “if I did care I'd knock
their heads together. I shall draw you till my mistress says give over.

“Luke, if you obey Kate, you will oblige me.”

“Then I will obey Kate.”

An honourable exception to popular humour was Jorian Ketel's wife. “That
is strength well laid out, to draw the weak. And her prayers will be
your guerdon; she is not long for this world; she smileth in pain.”
 These were the words of Joan.

Single-minded Luke answered that he did not want the poor lass's prayers
he did it to please his mistress, Margaret.

After that Luke often pressed Margaret to give him something to
do--without success.

But one day, as if tired with his importuning, she turned on him, and
said with a look and accent I should in vain try to convey:

“Find me my boy's father.”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

"Eli," Catherine commanded, her voice cutting through the domestic haze with the precision of a surgeon's blade, "answer me one question like a man, and I shall ask no more today. What is wormwood?"

Eli faltered, momentarily paralyzed by the sudden demand upon his faculties, as if struck by a physical blow. Yet, he rallied quickly, offering a definition rooted in mere sensation rather than spirit. "It is something that tastes main bitter."

"That is a fair answer, my man, but not the one I seek," she replied, her eyes hardening.

"Then answer it yourself," he challenged, retreating behind the shield of his ignorance.

"And shall," Eli grunted, the weight of her scrutiny pressing down on him. "Wormwood is—to have two in the house a-doing nought, but waiting for thy shoes and mine."

The shaft struck home with devastating accuracy. Catherine's expression hardened further. "Methinks waiting for their best friend's coffin, that and nothing to do, are enow to make them worse than Nature meant. Why not set them up somewhere, to give 'em a chance?"

Eli hesitated, admitting his willingness but voicing a fear born of experience: "But I am afraid they will drink and gamble their very shelves away."

"Nay," Catherine countered, her tone leaving no room for doubt. "Dost thou take me for a simpleton? Of course I mean to watch them at the starting, and drive them with a loose rein, as the saying is." Her gaze sharpened, piercing the veil of his hesitation. "Where didst thou think of doing this? Not here; to divide our own custom."

"Not likely," Eli muttered. "I say Rotterdam against the world. Then I could start them."

Oh, self-deception! The true motive driving this entire maneuver was not merely commerce, but the desperate, aching proximity to little Gerard. Following many heated discussions and eager promises of amendment on these specific terms, Catherine departed for Rotterdam, accompanied by Kate, to hunt for a shop. Seeking a change of air and purpose, they soon located a premises in a respectable street, though it stood sadly out of order. Undeterred, they seized the opportunity; the dilapidation allowed them to secure it at a fraction of the cost. Instantly, they set to work, scrubbing the floors until they gleamed, fitting proper shelves for the burgeoning business, and rendering the dwelling-house habitable once more.

Meanwhile, Luke Peterson found himself constantly approaching Margaret, inquiring what he might do to assist her. Her response invariably fell in a tone laden with sorrowful resignation: "Nothing, Luke, nothing."

"What, you that are so clever, can you think of nothing for me to do for you?" he pleaded, his hope flickering like a candle in a draft.

"Nothing, Luke, nothing," she repeated, closing herself off.

But eventually, she varied her reply, opening a narrow crack in her defenses: "If you could make something to help my sweet sister Kate about."

The slave of love, consumed by devotion, consented joyfully. Soon, Luke had fashioned a small cart for Kate, cushioning it with care, and even yoked himself into it. At eventide, he drew her out of the town and along the pleasant boulevard, with Margaret and Catherine walking beside them. On the surface, it appeared a happier party than reality warranted. Kate, however, enjoyed the moment keenly; little Gerard was placed in her lap, and she doted on him with a tenderness that transformed the scene into something ethereal—a cherub carried by a little angel, or a rosebud resting in the cup of a lily.

Yet, beneath this fragile peace, the vulgar jeered. They mocked Luke, asking how a thistle tasted and questioning whether his mistress could not afford a horse with four legs instead of a man. Luke did not mind these taunts; he bore them with stoic silence. But Kate minded them for him.

"Thou hast made the cart for me, good Luke," she said, her voice trembling slightly. "'Twas much. I did ill to let thee draw me too; we can afford to pay some poor soul for that. I love my rides, and to carry little Gerard; but I'd liever ride no more than thou be mocked for't."

"Much I care for their tongues," Luke declared, his jaw set in defiance. "If I did care, I'd knock their heads together. I shall draw you till my mistress says give over."

"Luke, if you obey Kate, you will oblige me," Margaret interjected softly.

"Then I will obey Kate," Luke affirmed.

An honorable exception to the prevailing mockery was Jorian Ketel's wife, Joan. She spoke with a prophetic gravity that silenced the crowd. "That is strength well laid out, to draw the weak. And her prayers will be your guerdon; she is not long for this world; she smileth in pain."

These were the words of Joan, speaking of death and suffering. Single-minded Luke, however, dismissed such spiritual currency. "I do not want the poor lass's prayers," he stated firmly. "I do it to please my mistress, Margaret."

After that, Luke often pressed Margaret to give him something substantial to do, without success. But one day, seemingly tired of his persistent importuning, she turned on him. With a look and an accent that conveyed a depth of emotion I should in vain try to convey, she delivered her final command: "Find me my boy's father."
